title: Indian-American Doctor Amish Shah Wins Arizona Congressional Primary, Defying Party Establishment
excerpt: The emergency room physician and son of Indian immigrants defeated the national Democratic Party's preferred candidate to secure a nomination in one of the most consequential US House races of 2026.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Amish Shah won the Arizona Democratic primary on July 22, 2026, despite party opposition.
  • Over $1.5 million was spent against Shah, making it one of Arizona's costliest primaries.
  • Shah will face Republican Jay Feely in the November 3 general election.
  • He previously lost to David Schweikert by a narrow 52-48% margin in 2024.
  • Shah's victory signifies growing Indian-American representation in U.S. politics.

A Victory Against the Machine

Amish Shah, an Indian-American emergency room physician, won the Democratic primary in Arizona's 1st Congressional District on Tuesday, overcoming millions of dollars in opposition spending and the rare intervention of his own party's national leadership, which had backed his rival.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2080123003489386971

The Associated Press called the race for Shah at 7:07 p.m. on July 22, one day after the election. He held a commanding lead over Marlene Galán-Woods, a former television news anchor who carried endorsements from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Planned Parenthood's campaign arm, US Senator Mark Kelly, and Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes.

Outside groups spent more than $1.5 million opposing Shah and over $1 million in supportive ads for Galán-Woods, making it one of the most expensive primary contests in the state's history. Shah's victory was met with relief and jubilation at his election night gathering in Scottsdale.

"I hope that I can get their endorsement over Jay Feely."

— Amish Shah, on seeking the DCCC's support after defeating their preferred candidate

From India to the Emergency Room to Congress

Shah's parents were engineering students who immigrated from India in the 1960s. His father is Jain and his mother is Hindu. Born and raised in Chicago, Shah attended Catholic school before graduating cum laude from Northwestern University with a degree in economics. He went on to Northwestern's medical school, earned a Master's in Public Health at UC Berkeley, and completed his emergency medicine residency at New York City's busiest Level I trauma centre.

He taught at Mount Sinai Medical Center, led the New York Jets Airway Management Team, and helped the NFL improve its emergency protocols. After a fellowship at the University of Arizona, he settled in the state and became board-certified in both emergency medicine and sports medicine. He speaks fluent Gujarati alongside conversational Spanish.

In 2019, Shah became the first Indian-American elected to the Arizona state legislature. A visit to Mahatma Gandhi's home in India had inspired his turn to public service. During his time in the Arizona House, he had more bills signed into law than any other Democrat in over a decade, earning a reputation for bipartisan pragmatism.

The Stakes in November

Arizona's 1st Congressional District—covering Scottsdale, Paradise Valley, and a broad swath of north Phoenix—is one of a handful of seats nationwide that will determine whether Republicans hold their slim House majority through the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.

Incumbent Republican David Schweikert, who defeated Shah by a 52-48% margin in 2024, did not seek re-election and is instead running for governor. The Republican primary was won by Jay Feely, a former Arizona Cardinals kicker who secured Trump's endorsement.

Shah told reporters he intends to win over the national Democratic apparatus that opposed him. "To know that people could see through the attack ads, and that being mean didn't work anymore, is honestly a relief," said Heather Mrowiec, treasurer of Shah's campaign.

What's Next

The general election is set for November 3, 2026. Shah will need to pivot quickly to compete in a district that has leaned Republican since 2020 but has remained competitive. For the Indian-American community—one of the fastest-growing political constituencies in the United States—Shah's candidacy represents another landmark in a growing wave of representation at the federal level. His primary victory, achieved against his own party's machinery, may prove to be the easier fight.
